questions.def: "Few" is used for countable nouns and implies a small number.
questions.question: ___ of the applicants had the required experience.

questions.def: "Little" is used with uncountable nouns like "evidence".
questions.question: There was ___ evidence to support his claim.

questions.def: "Much" is for uncountable nouns; use "many" for people.
questions.question: Much people attended the conference yesterday.

questions.def: "A number of" is followed by a plural noun.
questions.question: Only a ___ of students passed the exam.

questions.def: "Limited" correctly describes the amount of time available.
questions.question: He has ___ time to dedicate to this project.

questions.def: "Some" is used for a portion of uncountable nouns.
questions.question: ___ of the information was useful for the report.

questions.def: "Percentage" refers to a proportion out of 100.
questions.question: A small ___ of employees were late.

questions.def: "Several" implies more than a few, less than many.
questions.question: ___ students failed the test; most passed.

questions.def: "No" is the correct quantifier to express absence.
questions.question: I have ___ patience for such nonsense.

questions.def: "Any" should be "None" for a negative meaning.
questions.question: Any of the candidates are qualified enough.

questions.def: "Amount" is used with uncountable nouns like money.
questions.question: A large ___ of money was stolen.

questions.def: "Most" indicates a majority of a countable noun.
questions.question: ___ of the cakes were eaten.

questions.def: "A lot of" works for both countable/uncountable nouns.
questions.question: He drank ___ water after the marathon.

questions.def: "Quantity" refers to an amount of something.
questions.question: A small ___ of sugar is enough.

questions.def: "Few" suggests a small number and negative sentiment.
questions.question: ___ of the employees are satisfied with their salaries.

questions.def: "Several" is appropriate for a number greater than few.
questions.question: ___ of the apples were rotten.

questions.def: "Much" is fine with uncountable "work" here.
questions.question: Much of the work remains to be done.

questions.def: "Portion" is suitable here, meaning a part of the whole.
questions.question: Only a small ___ of the land is fertile.

questions.def: "Much" modifies the uncountable noun "research".
questions.question: ___ of the research is still ongoing.

questions.def: "Numerous" means a large number; it's for countable nouns.
questions.question: There are ___ opportunities available in this field.

questions.def: "Every" needs a singular noun: "student".
questions.question: Every students must submit their essay.

questions.def: "Majority" is the correct noun form.
questions.question: The ___ of students passed the exam.

questions.def: "A few" indicates a small but positive number of people.
questions.question: Only ___ people knew the secret.

questions.def: "Little" is used with the uncountable noun "choice" here.
questions.question: He had ___ choice but to accept the offer.

questions.def: "Sufficient" is the adjective form, meaning enough.
questions.question: There is not ___ evidence to convict him.

questions.def: "Most of" precedes a determiner + noun (the students).
questions.question: ___ the students passed the test with flying colors.

questions.def: "Hardly any" expresses a very small quantity of uncountable nouns.
questions.question: There is ___ sugar left in the jar.

questions.def: 'A minority' is the correct quantifier for a small proportion.
questions.question: ___ of the applicants had the required experience.

questions.def: 'Quite a few' means a surprising number; 'fewly' is not a word.
questions.question: ___ students failed the exam, which was unexpected.

questions.def: Use 'many' with countable nouns like 'people,' not 'much'.
questions.question: Much people believe that the climate is changing.
